An online interactive physics-informed diffusion-adversarial network for solving mean field games
Article preview
Abstract

abstract:
Abstract
High-dimensional, complex, and dynamic environments pose significant challenges in solving mean field games (MFGs). To address these challenges, we propose an online interactive physics-informed diffusion-adversarial network (IPIDAN), which offers enhanced interpretability and flexibility by leveraging a novel agent strategy generator based on diffusion models. This generator utilizes a noise process to improve its ability to escape local optima, while a stepwise optimization process during the denoising phase generates refined agent strategies, thereby enhancing the quality and diversity of the generated results. The discriminator perceives the distribution and strategies of agents in MFGs by extracting the physical information exchange from agent interactions. By using variational techniques, the typical MFG problem is transformed into a static optimization problem, which is then efficiently approximated using a generative adversarial framework through adversarial training. IPIDAN, with its diffusion generation model architecture, provides the network with greater tunability and significantly enhances its ability to model randomness in high-dimensional strategy spaces. Furthermore, by establishing a connection between the diffusion process and the agents’ motion dynamics, the network achieves improved interpretability and robustness. Numerical experiments and comparisons with experimental results validate the effectiveness of the novel agent strategy generator based on diffusion models, particularly demonstrating its superior performance through quadrotor obstacle avoidance experiments conducted in various complex scenarios.

  - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
  - generic: MFGs are an important theoretical tool for studying the dynamic equilibrium of large populations of rational agents. This framework transforms high-dimensional interaction problems, which are difficult to handle in traditional game theory, into analyzable systems of partial differential equations using continuous medium approximation methods. They were independently proposed by Caines et al. [1] and Lasry et al. [2] in 2006. In practical applications, they have been used to solve complex decision-making and game theory problems, such as in economic research [3] and social sciences [4], [5].

  - generic: In the mathematical foundation research of the MFG system, scholars focus on core theoretical issues such as the existence, uniqueness, and structural preservation of solutions. Achdou and Capuzzo-Dolcetta [7] developed numerical methods for stationary and evolutive MFGs, analyzing existence and uniqueness of discrete solutions. Achdou et al. [8] introduced a semi-implicit finite difference scheme and a Newton iteration for optimal planning in MFGs. Benamou and Carlier [9] established an augmented Lagrangian framework for regularizing Monge optimal transport via variational inequalities. Liu et al. [10], [11] showed that non-degenerate MFGs can be reformulated as monotone inclusion problems, supporting convex optimization approaches. Arias and Kalise [12], [13] proposed a finite difference scheme for stationary MFGs, recasting the discrete system as a variational optimization problem. N. Almulla et al. [14] developed a gradient flow-based numerical method for smooth MFGs, emphasizing variational properties and monotonicity. Andreev [15] introduced a preconditioner using augmented Lagrangian and multigrid techniques for efficient solution of instationary MFGs with diffusion. Yu et al. [16] extended MFGs to Riemannian manifolds and proposed a proximal gradient method for geometric PDEs. Li et al. [17] developed a multiscale alternating sweeping method for efficient MFG solutions on refined grids. Mou et al. [18] proposed meshless algorithms for MFGs using Gaussian processes and random Fourier features, improving efficiency and convergence. Huang et al. [19] linked MFGs with normalizing flows, enabling accurate high-dimensional solutions via trajectory-based neural parameterization. Agrawal et al. [20] proposed a random features framework for high-dimensional nonlocal MFGs, efficiently approximating interaction kernels in feature space and enabling flexible trajectory optimization extensions. Recently, significant progress has been made in inverse problems for MFGs. Liu and Lo [31] established unique identifiability results for the topological structures and parameter configurations of state space anomalies, while Ding et al. [32] proposed an enhanced higher-order linearization method to uniquely identify system parameters from full or partial boundary measurements.
  - generic: Machine learning methods have recently gained widespread attention and research. In the field of generative diffusion models, Sohl-Dickstein et al. [21] pioneered the use of nonequilibrium thermodynamics for deep unsupervised learning. They introduced a framework that leverages forward and reverse diffusion processes to model data distributions. Building on this foundation, Ho et al. [22] proposed denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). These models significantly improved the efficiency and quality of sample generation through a simplified noise scheduling mechanism. Further advancing this research, Song et al. [23] introduced score-based generative modeling via stochastic differential equations. This approach unified diffusion models and score matching under a single mathematical framework. These works collectively establish the theoretical and practical foundations of diffusion-based generative modeling, providing a robust basis for applications in high-dimensional data generation and optimization problems.
  - generic: Machine learning methods have been applied to solve MFGs, promoting the rapid development of numerical methods for solving Eq. (1.1). Cao et al. [24] explored the connections between GANs, MFGs, and Optimal Transport. They proposed using two neural networks to solve the HJB equation and the FPK equation through adversarial training to address MFG models. Ruthotto et al. [25] proposed a machine learning framework for solving high-dimensional MFG and MFC problems. By combining Lagrangian and Eulerian viewpoints and leveraging neural network parameterization, their method avoids spatial discretization. Lin et al. [26] proposed APAC-Net, a neural network framework for solving high-dimensional stochastic MFGs. It uses neural networks to parameterize value and density functions. Lauriére et al. [27] provide a comprehensive survey on the integration of reinforcement learning (RL) with mean field games (MFGs). They explore how RL can address large-scale MFG problems in a model-free manner, offering insights into learning equilibria and social optima in complex environments.
  - generic: "Yin et al. [28] proposed an online interactive physical information adversarial network (IPIAN) to address the MFG problem from the perspective of physical information interaction. This method effectively solves high-dimensional MFG models using an adversarial network framework and self-attention mechanisms. The advantage of this approach lies in its incorporation of attention mechanisms to focus on policy features and establish long-range dependencies through self-attention, thereby enhancing training efficiency. However, the method still has limitations: 1) The generator based on conventional convolutional networks often suffers from mode collapse, failing to capture the full diversity of the optimal strategy distribution. 2) The controllability of the convolutional generator’s output is relatively low, and the diversity of results is insufficient."
  - generic: "This study proposes IPIDAN for solving MFG problems in high-dimensional, complex, and dynamic environments. By exploring the physical correspondence between the forward and reverse processes of diffusion models and the agent motion solving process in MFG systems, the DI-WGAN framework is constructed. It integrates Wasserstein generative adversarial networks with diffusion models. Specifically, IPIDAN has the following innovative features:"
  - generic: "1) A group strategy generator based on diffusion models: It expands the search range at high noise levels to escape local optima and progressively refines details at low noise levels to achieve fine-grained strategy reconstruction, significantly improving generation accuracy and efficiency."
  - generic: "2) A physics-informed interactive discriminator: It incorporates the MFG governing equations (specifically the HJB residuals) as physics-informed constraints within the discriminator’s loss function, ensuring the learned value function adheres to the underlying system dynamics."
  - generic: "3) Variational dyadic structure optimization: It utilizes the variational properties of MFGs to transform dynamic game problems into static optimization problems, achieving efficient solutions through adversarial training."
  - generic: Compared to traditional methods, IPIDAN provides a more refined parameter tuning space through the diffusion generation model architecture. It enhances the ability to model stochastic features in high-dimensional strategy spaces. Particularly, compared to the previously proposed IPIAN method, IPIDAN addresses the mode collapse issue of convolutional generators. It significantly improves the diversity and controllability of results through the progressive generation process of diffusion models. Numerical experiments validate the superior performance of this method in solving high-dimensional MFG problems, especially demonstrating significant advantages in quadrotor obstacle avoidance tasks in complex dynamic scenarios.
